clinicalPearls: Occlusion characteristically occurs at an arteriovenous crossing, where the artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath, so the resulting signs are confined to the sector drained by the affected vein
The superotemporal quadrant is most commonly involved, producing a quadrantic wedge of flame-shaped haemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins and cotton-wool spots that respects the horizontal raphe
Systemic hypertension is the single commonest association, and its presence should be actively sought in every case
Macular oedema is the principal cause of reduced central vision and is best characterised and monitored with optical coherence tomography
Retinal ischaemia (capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography) may drive later retinal or disc neovascularisation and vitreous haemorrhage

Management centres on treating macular oedema with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy or macular laser, applying sectoral laser to ischaemic retina with neovascularisation, and controlling cardiovascular risk factors
In patients under fifty, inflammatory and thrombophilic causes should be considered rather than assuming simple arteriosclerotic disease
reference.pathophysiology: At an arteriovenous crossing the retinal artery and vein are enclosed within a shared adventitial sheath, so age-related arteriolar wall thickening compresses the underlying vein. The resulting turbulence and endothelial injury promote local thrombosis and venous outflow obstruction. Pressure rises in the venules and capillaries upstream of the block, producing haemorrhage, plasma leakage with macular oedema, and variable capillary non-perfusion within the drained sector. Ischaemic retina releases vascular endothelial growth factor, which aggravates oedema and can stimulate later neovascularisation.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to map the sectoral distribution of haemorrhage and identify the culprit crossing
Optical coherence tomography of the macula to detect and quantify macular oedema
Fluorescein angiography to assess capillary non-perfusion, macular ischaemia and any neovascularisation
Blood pressure measurement and cardiovascular risk assessment
Fasting glucose or HbA1c and a lipid profile
Thrombophilia and inflammatory screen in younger patients or bilateral disease
redFlags: Retinal or disc neovascularisation with vitreous haemorrhage
Neovascular glaucoma with a painful red eye and raised intraocular pressure
Occlusion in a young patient, prompting a search for inflammatory or thrombophilic causes
Profound or worsening central visual loss from macular ischaemia
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable and depends largely on macular perfusion; many non-ischaemic eyes retain useful vision, whereas persistent macular oedema or macular ischaemia limits recovery, and untreated ischaemic disease may progress to neovascular complications.
pitfalls: Attributing the occlusion to age alone without checking and treating blood pressure
Missing peripheral capillary non-perfusion and early neovascularisation on angiography
Overlooking macular oedema that is apparent only on optical coherence tomography
Failing to arrange ongoing review for late neovascular complications
